windows.head.meta-content1: Install the unsigned Windows preview of the OpenWalkieTalkie app and service, get past SmartScreen, and update your deck's firmware over USB.
windows.head.meta-content2: Install the unsigned Windows preview of the OpenWalkieTalkie app and service.
windows.content.p2: The app and service for Windows 10 and 11 on x64
windows.content.p3: The Windows preview runs the same service and app as the Mac: your deck links over USB-C or Bluetooth, shows your Claude Code and Codex sessions, answers their approvals, takes push-to-talk dictation and speaks replies, and the app updates the deck’s firmware. It is a preview because a few Mac features are not on Windows (below), and it is not code-signed, so Windows warns before it runs it the first time.
windows.content.p4: Download the Windows x64 preview ZIP. This standalone Windows preview includes voice, Claude Code, Codex CLI and Grok Bot. Its release notes list the source revision and SHA-256 checksum. Full releases from 0.14.0 on also include Windows builds named OpenWalkieTalkie-<version>-windows-x86_64.zip. To verify your download, run this in PowerShell in your Downloads folder:
windows.content.li1: Unzip it somewhere you keep programs, for example %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\OpenWalkieTalkie. Keep the bin folder as it is: the app installs firmware only when it runs from a folder named bin, and it starts the deckd.exe beside it.
windows.content.li2: Open bin\OpenWalkieTalkie.exe. Windows SmartScreen shows Windows protected your PC, because the program is not signed. Choose More info, then Run anyway. Windows remembers the choice for this copy.
windows.content.li3: Follow the first-run steps. They start deckd.exe, the service that talks to the deck, in the background with no window, and set it to start whenever you sign in (Settings › Apps › Startup lists it). Service › Start at login does the same for the app. Closing the window keeps the app in the notification area; its icon’s menu quits it.
windows.content.li4: Connect the deck with USB-C, or pair it in Settings › Bluetooth & devices. The app’s Deck page shows it once the service has linked.
windows.content.p5: Push to talk on the deck is heard by Whisper, on this PC: download its model on the app’s Voice page (Windows has no recogniser of its own, so a press says so until the model is in). Replies are spoken by Windows’ own voice unless you choose Kokoro (downloaded the same way) or a cloud voice with your own OpenAI or ElevenLabs key. The deck’s microphone and speaker work over the cable and over Bluetooth.
windows.content.h31: If Windows does not offer “Run anyway”
windows.content.p6: Smart App Control, on some new Windows 11 installations, blocks unsigned programs and gives no way past it. You can see its setting in Windows Security → App & browser control → Smart App Control. The preview cannot run while it is on, and on many Windows versions it cannot be turned back on without reinstalling Windows once it is off, so decide whether that is worth it for you. Antivirus software may also hold back a new unsigned download for a while; the checksum above tells you it is the file the release published.
windows.content.p7: With one deck connected by USB-C, open Service, click Check on Deck firmware, then Review… and Install, exactly as on the Mac. Keep the cable connected until the deck is back. On Windows the transfer uses the deck’s HID connection rather than its faster USB interface, which Windows has no driver for, so it takes a few minutes (about five for 0.13.0 on Rev A). If you run Windows in a virtual machine, make sure the deck is passed through again after it restarts: it reconnects twice during an update.
windows.content.p8: Grok Bot: open Integrations → Bots to add a bot's routine webhook. Copy Prompt gives the bot PowerShell commands to send replies and questions back to this PC; allow those commands in Grok Bot's Computer settings. The service keeps routine keys in Windows Credential Manager. A service on a separate data directory uses grokbot-keys.toml instead.
windows.content.p9: Open Service and click Check beside the app, or choose Check for Updates… from the icon’s menu. When the latest release has a newer version, click Update: the app downloads the release’s zip, checks it against the checksums the release publishes, puts the new OpenWalkieTalkie.exe and deckd.exe in your bin folder, and starts again. Your settings stay in %LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenWalkieTalkie. To update by hand instead, download the zip from the latest release, quit the app from its icon, and replace the old version’s folder with the new one.
windows.content.li5: The cloud voice’s key is kept in Windows Credential Manager, where the Mac keeps it in the Keychain.
windows.content.li6: The app is unsigned, so the service trusts it by where it is: the OpenWalkieTalkie.exe beside deckd.exe. A Mac checks the app’s signature instead.
windows.content.li7: Not on Windows yet: the MLX voice, which needs Apple silicon, and the launcher that opens Codex Desktop on the service’s shared Codex daemon. Codex in the terminal works as on the Mac.
windows.content.p10: Run bin\deckd.exe uninstall to stop the service, remove the start-at-sign-in entries and the Claude Code and Codex integrations; add --purge to delete what is in %LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenWalkieTalkie too (settings, voice models, downloaded firmware), all but its logs folder, which you can delete yourself. Then quit the app from its icon and delete the folder you unzipped.
windows.content.p11: Something not working? Open an issue with the log from %LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenWalkieTalkie\logs.
